''var.'' araneosa|[[Cornelis Gijsbert Gerrit Jan van Steenis|Steenis]] }} }} '''''Caltha palustris''''', known as '''marsh-marigold'''{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}} and '''kingcup''', is a small to medium sized [[perennial]] [[herbaceous]] [[flowering plant|plant]] of the [[buttercup family]], [[native plant|native]] to [[marsh]]es, [[fen]]s, ditches and wet [[woodland]] in [[temperate]] regions of the [[Northern Hemisphere]]. It flowers between April and August, dependent on altitude and latitude, but occasional flowers may occur at other times. == Description == ''Caltha palustris'' is a {{convert|10|–|80|cm|frac=2}} high, hairless, fleshy, perennial, herbaceous plant that dies down in autumn and [[Raunkiær plant life-form#Cryptophytes|overwinters with buds near the surface of the marshy soil]]. The plants have many, {{convert|2|–|3|mm|frac=32}} thick strongly branching roots. Its flowering stems are hollow, erect or more or less decumbent. The [[alternate leaf|alternate]] true leaves are in a [[Rosette (botany)|rosette]], each of which consist of a [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] that is about four times as long as the [[wikt:Reniform|kidney-shaped]] [[leaf blade]], which is between {{cvt|3|–|25|cm|frac=4}} long and {{cvt|3|–|20|cm|frac=4}} wide. The leaf possesses a heart-shaped foot, a blunt tip, and a scalloped to toothed, sometime almost entire margin particularly towards the tip. In their youth the leaves are protected by a membranous sheath, that may be up to {{cvt|3|cm|frac=4}} long in fully grown plants. === Inflorescence === The common marsh-marigold mostly has several [[Peduncle (botany)|flowering stems]] of up to {{cvt|80|cm}} long, carrying mostly several [[Sessility (botany)|seated]] leaflike [[stipule]]s, although lower ones may be on a short petiole; and between four and six (but occasionally as few as one or as many as 25) flowers. The flowers are approximately {{cvt|4|cm|frac=4}} but range between {{cvt|2|–|5.5|cm|frac=4}} in diameter. There are four to nine (mostly five) petal-like, brightly colored (yolk yellow, white or magenta), inverted egg-shaped [[sepal]]s, each about {{cvt|1.75|cm|frac=4}} but ranging from {{cvt|1|–|2.5|cm|frac=4}} long, and about {{cvt|1.33|cm|frac=4}}, ranging from {{cvt|0.75|–|1.75|cm|frac=4}} wide; they have a blunt or sometimes acute tip. Real [[petal]]s and [[nectar]]ies are lacking. Between 50 and 120 [[stamen]]s with flattened yellow filaments and yellow [[tricolpate]] or sometimes pantoporate [[pollen]] encircle 5–25 free, flattened, linear-oblong, yellow to green [[carpel]]s, with a two-lobed, obliquely positioned [[Stigma (botany)|stigma]], and each with many [[Ovule|seedbuds]]. This later develops into a seated, funnel-shaped fruit (a so-called [[follicle (fruit)|follicle]]) of {{cvt|0.75|–|2|cm|frac=4}} long and {{cvt|0.25|–|0.5|cm|frac=8}} wide, that opens with one suture at the side of the axis and contains 7–20 ovoid, brown to black seeds of about {{cvt|2.5|×|1.5|mm|frac=32}}. == Taxonomy == === Taxonomic history === The oldest [[Species description|description]] that is generally acknowledged in the botanical literature dates from 1700 under the name ''Populago'' by [[Joseph Pitton de Tournefort]] in [https://books.google.nl/books/reader?id=2BkOAAAAQAAJ&hl=nl&printsec=frontcover&output=reader&source=gbs_atb_hover&pg=GBS.PA273 part 1 of his Institutiones rei herbariae]. He distinguished between ''P. flore major'', ''P. flore minor'' and ''P. flore plena'', and already says all of these are synonymous to ''Caltha palustris'', without mentioning any previous author. As a plant name published before 1 May 1753, ''Populago'' Tourn. is [[Validly published name|invalid]]. And so is the first description as ''Caltha palustris'' by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in his [[Genera Plantarum]] of 1737. But Linnaeus re-describes the species under the same name in [[Species Plantarum]] of 1 May 1753, thus providing the [[Correct name (botany)|correct name]].{{cite book|first= C.E.|last= Moss|year= 1920|title= The Cambridge British Flora|volume= III|pages= 104–105|publisher= CUP Archive}} === Etymology === [[Image:Caltha palustris (navadna kalužnica).jpg|thumb|A ''Caltha palustris'' flower and bud at the [[Ljubljana Botanical Garden]] in [[Slovenia]]]] The generic name ''Caltha'' is derived from the [[Ancient Greek]] {{lang|grc|κάλαθος}} ({{grc-tr|κάλαθος}}), meaning "goblet", and is said to refer to the shape of the flower.{{cite web|website= New Zealand Plant Conservation Network|title= Caltha novae-zelandiae|author= P.J. de Lange|access-date= 2016-01-11|url= http://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora_details.aspx?ID=1203}} The species [[epithet]] ''palustris'' is Latin for "of the marsh" and indicates its common habitat.Archibald William Smith {{google books|ahNMkgoNJ7IC|A Gardener's Handbook of Plant Names: Their Meanings and Origins|page=258}} In the UK, ''Caltha palustris'' is known by a variety of vernacular names, varying by geographical region. These include in addition to the most common two, marsh marigold and kingcup, also brave bassinets, crazy Beth, horse blob,{{Cn|date=May 2021}} Molly-blob,{{cite web |url=https://en.oxforddictionaries.com/definition/molly-blob |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190417153624/https://en.oxforddictionaries.com/definition/molly-blob |url-status=dead |archive-date=April 17, 2019 |title = MOLLY-BLOB {{!}} Meaning & Definition for UK English {{!}} Lexico.com}} May blob, mare blob, boots, water boots, meadow-bright, bullflower, meadow buttercup, water buttercup, soldier's buttons, meadow cowslip, water cowslip, publican's cloak, crowfoot, water dragon, drunkards, water goggles, meadow gowan, water gowan, yellow gowan, goldes, golds, goldings, gools, cow lily, marybuds, and publicans-and-sinners.{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector – ''Caltha palustris''|url=http://apps.rhs.org.uk/plantselector/plant?plantid=295|archive-url=https://archive.today/20121224032811/http://apps.rhs.org.uk/plantselector/plant?plantid=295|url-status=dead|archive-date=December 24, 2012|access-date=20 June 2013}} The common name "marigold" refers to its use in medieval churches at Easter as a tribute to the Virgin Mary, as in "Mary gold". In North America ''Caltha palustris'' is sometimes known as cowslip. However, cowslip more often refers to ''[[Primula veris]]'', the original plant to go by that name.{{cite web | url = http://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/cowslip|title = cowslip|work = Merriam-Webster Online Dictionary}}{{Better source|date=May 2021}} Both are herbaceous plants with yellow flowers, but ''Primula veris'' is much smaller.{{Cn|date=May 2021}} === Subdivision, synonymy and culture varieties === [[File:White marsh marigold 01.jpg|thumb|upright|White form seen in the Himalayas in Kashmir, India]] ''Caltha palustris'' is a very [[Phenotype|variable]] species. Since most [[Phenotypic trait|character states]] occur in almost any combination, this provides little basis for subdivisions. The following varieties are nevertheless widely recognised. They are listed with their respective [[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonyms]]. Double flowered: "Flore Pleno" (RHS's [[Award of Garden Merit]]), "Multiplex", "Plena", "Semiplena". == Distribution and habitat == [[File:Caltha palustris in Himachal Pradesh, India, photographed by Yogabrata Chakraborty, on June 3, 2023.jpg|thumb|200px|Closeup view of Caltha palustris in [[Himachal Pradesh]], India.]] The species is [[native plant|native]] to [[marsh]]es, [[fen]]s, ditches and wet [[woodland]] in [[temperate]] regions of the [[Northern Hemisphere]]. It can be found in much of the northeastern United States.{{Cite book |title=The Complete Guide to Edible Wild Plants |publisher=[[Skyhorse Publishing]] |others=[[United States Department of the Army]] |year=2009 |isbn=978-1-60239-692-0 |location=New York |pages=68 |language=en-US |oclc=277203364}} == Ecology == [[File:Łomżyński Park Krajobrazowy Doliny Narwi, wiosenne rozlewiska, kaczeńce.jpg|thumb|The marsh-marigold on [[Spring (season)|spring]] [[flood plain]]s of the [[Narew]] river.]] The marsh-marigold grows in places with oxygen-rich water near the surface of the soil. It likes richer soils, but dislikes application of [[fertilizer]] and avoids high concentrations of [[phosphate]] and [[ammonium]], and is also shy of brackish water. It is often associated with seepage that is rich in iron, because iron ions react with phosphate, thus making it unavailable for plants. The resulting [[insoluble]] mineral appears as "rusty" [[flocs]] on the water soil and the surface of the stems of marsh plants. Around the [[Riparian zone|edge]] of lakes and rivers it grows between [[Phragmites|reeds]], and it can be found in [[black alder]] [[coppice]]s and other regularly flooded and always moist forests. When it is present it often visually dominates when it is in bloom. It also used to be common on wet [[meadow]]s, but due to agricultural rationalization it is now limited to ditches.{{cite book|author1=E.J. Weeda |author2=R. Westra |author3=C. Westra |author4=T. Westra |year= 1985|title= Nederlandse Oecologische Flora|volume= 1|pages= 226–229|publisher= IVN}} It is a component of [[purple moor grass and rush pastures]] – a type of [[Biodiversity Action Plan]] habitat in the UK. It occurs on poorly drained neutral and acidic soils of the lowlands and upland fringe.{{Cn|date=May 2021}} In western Europe, the marsh-marigold moth ''[[Micropterix calthella]]'' bites open the [[anther]]s of the marsh-marigold and other plants to eat the [[pollen]]. The [[caterpillar]]s that are present in summer and autumn also feed on marsh-marigold, although these are sometimes found on mosses too. Another visitor of ''Caltha palustris'' in western Europe is the leaf beetle ''Prasocuris phellandrii'', which is black with four orange stripes and around ½ cm and eats the sepals. Its larvae inhabit the hollow stems of members of the parsley family. In the USA (Illinois) two species of leaf beetle can be found on Caltha: ''Plateumaris nitida'' and ''Hydrothassa vittata''.{{Illinois Wildflowers|wetland/plants/marsh_marigold|Marsh Marigold (Caltha palustris) |access-date=2016-01-29}} The maggots of some ''Phytomyza'' species ([[Agromyzidae]]) are miners in ''Caltha'' leaves.{{cite book|author= George C. Steyskal|title= Keys to The Insects of The European Part of The USSR|date= 1989|volume= 5|pages= 494, 500–501|publisher= Brill Archives|isbn= 978-9004090262}} === Pollination === [[Image:Sphegina montana Syrphidae.jpg|thumb|''Caltha palustris'' pollination by a syrphid fly (''[[Sphegina montana]]'')]] The flowers produce both nectar and copious amounts of pollen which attract many insect visitors. They may be most commonly pollinated by hoverflies (Syrphidae).{{cite web|author= Sue Trull|website= USDA – Plant of the week|title= Yellow Marsh Marigold|url= http://www.fs.fed.us/wildflowers/plant-of-the-week/caltha_palustris.shtml|access-date= 2016-02-13}} In Canada, beetles ([[Cantharidae]], [[Nitidulidae]], [[Coccinellidae]], [[Chrysomelidae]], [[Cerambycidae]]), thrips ([[Thripidae]]), bugs ([[Miridae]]), butterflies ([[Pieridae]]), sawflies ([[Tenthredinidae]]), bees ([[Apidae]], [[Halictidae]], [[Andrenidae]]), ants ([[Formicidae]]) and flies ([[Sepsidae]], [[Sciomyzidae]], [[Ephydridae]], [[Syrphidae]], [[Anthomyiidae]], [[Tachinidae]] and [[Muscidae]]) have been observed to visit the leaves or flowers, many of which were found carrying ''Caltha'' pollen.{{cite journal|first= W.W.|last= Judd|year= 1964|title= Insects Associated with Flowering Marsh Marigold, Caltha palustris L., at London, Ontario|journal= The Canadian Entomologist|volume= 96|issue= 11|pages= 1472–1476|doi= 10.4039/Ent961472-11|s2cid= 83650928}} In addition to other forms of pollination, this plant is adapted to rain-[[pollination]]. ''Caltha palustris'' is infertile when self-pollinated. Rather high fertility in crosses between sibling plants suggest that this phenomenon is genetically regulated by several genes. This regulation mechanism also occurs in ''[[Ranunculus]]'' and as far as known only in these two genera.{{cite journal|first= Arne|last= Lundqvist|year= 1992|title= The self-incompatibility system in Caltha palustris (Ranunculaceae)|journal= Hereditas|volume= 117|issue= 2|pages= 145–151|doi= 10.1111/j.1601-5223.1992.tb00168.x|doi-access= free}} === Seed dispersal === In ''Caltha palustris'' up to two hundred seeds may be produced by each flower. When the follicles open, they form a "splash cup". When a raindrop hits one at the right angle, the walls are shaped such that the seeds are expelled. The seeds also have some spongy tissue that makes them float on water, until they wash up in a location that may be suitable for this species to grow.{{cite web|website= NatureGate|title= Marsh Marigold|url= http://www.luontoportti.com/suomi/en/kukkakasvit/marsh-marigold|access-date= 2016-02-14}} === Diseases === The marsh-marigold is affected by the [[Rust (fungus)|rust]] species ''Puccinia calthea'' and ''P. calthicola''.Peter Zwetko: ''[http://www.landesmuseum.at/pdf_frei_remote/BioEco_16_0001-0067.pdf Die Rostpilze Österreichs.] Supplement und Wirt-Parasit-Verzeichnis zur 2. Auflage des Catalogus Florae Austriae, III. Teil, Heft 1, Uredinales.'' (PDF; 1,8 MB). == Toxicity == ''Caltha'' contains several active substances of which the most important from a toxicological point of view is [[protoanemonin]]. Consumption of larger quantities of the plant may cause convulsions, burning of the throat, vomiting, bloody diarrhea, dizziness and fainting. Contact of the skin or [[mucous membrane]]s with the juices can cause blistering or inflammation, and gastric illness if ingested. Younger parts seem to contain less toxics and heating breaks these substances down. Small amounts of ''Caltha'' in hay do not cause problems when fed to husbandry, but larger quantities lead to gastric illness. Additionally, plants that live in raw water may carry toxic organisms which can be neutralized by cooking. == Uses == Early spring greens and buds of ''Caltha palustris'' are edible when cooked (but are poisonous when raw).{{Cite book|last1=Elias|first1=Thomas S.|title=Edible Wild Plants: A North American Field Guide to Over 200 Natural Foods|last2=Dykeman|first2=Peter A.|publisher=[[Sterling Publishing|Sterling]]|year=2009|isbn=978-1-4027-6715-9|location=New York|pages=100|oclc=244766414|orig-year=1982}} Young leaves or buds should be submerged a few times in fresh boiling water until barely tender, cut into bite-sized pieces, lightly salted, and served with melted butter and vinegar.{{NPIN|CAPA5|Caltha palustris |access-date=2016-01-17}} Very young flowerbuds have been prepared like capers and used as a spice. The common marsh marigold is planted as an ornamental throughout temperate regions in the world, and sometimes recommended for low maintenance wildlife gardens. The double-flowered cultivar 'Flore Pleno' has won the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/2805/Caltha-palustris-Flore-Pleno-(d)/Details | title = ''Caltha palustris'' 'Flore Pleno' | publisher = RHS | access-date = 12 April 2020}} == Culture == {{More citations needed section|date=May 2021}} ''Caltha palustris'' is a plant commonly mentioned in literature, including [[Shakespeare]]: :''Winking Marybuds begin'' :''To open their golden eyes'' (''[[Cymbeline]]'', ii. 3). It also appears in [[Charlotte Brontë]]'s ''[[Shirley (novel)|Shirley]]'': :''They both halted on the green brow of the Common: they looked down on the deep valley robed in May raiment; on varied meads, some pearled with daisies, and some golden with king-cups: to-day all this young verdure smiled clear in sunlight; transparent emerald and amber gleams played over it ''{{cite web |last=Brontë |first=Charlotte |date=8 July 2018 |title=Shirley, by Currer Bell |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=x3VbAAAAQAAJ |via=Google Books}} and in [[Thomas Hardy]]'s poem 'Overlooking the River Stour': :''Closed were the kingcups; and the mead/Dripped in monotonous green,/Though the day's morning sheen/Had shown it golden and honeybee'd''. ''Kingcup Cottage'' by [[Racey Helps]] is a children's book which features the plant. == References == {{Reflist|refs= Hagerup, O. 1950.
